newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian metals-Truck stir hits trade, shortage seen.
newsitem.headline: Indian metals-Truck stir hits trade, shortage seen.

text.p: An indefinite strike by truck operators across India, pressing for the withdrawal of a service charge and a rise in insurance premiums, has crippled trading in non-ferrous metals, dealers said on Wednesday.
"Trading in non-ferrous metals has steeply fallen to about 10-20 percent," Bombay Metals Exchange president Sharad Parikh said. "There are no physical deliveries."
Parikh said the movement of metals from ports to consuming centres had come to a halt and a shortage in their supply was most likely in the next few days.
Operators of more than two million trucks on Tuesday pulled their vehicles off Indian roads in protest over a 5.0 percent service tax proposed in the 1997/98 (April-March) budget.
They are also protesting against a decision by state-owned insurance companies to raise premiums between 300 and 400 percent.
Talks between government officials and leaders of All-India Motor Transport Congress, spearheading the strike, are on and metal dealers are hopeful it will be called off soon.
Dealers said the strike had aggravated the shortage of non-ferrous metals as their imports in March had been limited with fiscal 1996/97 coming to a close.
"London Metals Exchange (LME) prices had been firm and that made dealers hesitant in placing import orders in the recent past. So the pipeline now is almost empty," said a dealer.

With the difference between domestic prices and LME prices mounting, the state-owned Hindustan Copper Ltd and Hindustan Zinc Ltd have raised the prices of their products by 2,000 rupees per tonne and 1,000 rupees per tonne respectively.
Dealers said they expect a shortage in both copper and zinc supply in the next few days.
Non-ferrous metals trade and industry have also been unhappy with the government's five-year (1997/2002) export-import policy, announced on Monday, which they said had failed to provide any relief.
"We have been pressing for withdrawal of a ban on import of zinc ash and dross that go into the manufacture of ingots," Parikh said. "The policy has not touched the issue."
Parikh said the two-year-old ban, imposed on the grounds that the use of zinc ash and dross were creating pollution problems, nearly killed many small scale zinc ingot makers.
The small scale zinc ingot units, fighting a legal battle against the ban, deny the charge that they are causing pollution.
Keshubhai Shah, a zinc trader, said the secondary producers using ash and dross accounted for more than 20 percent of the total annual supply of around 220,000 tonnes of the metal.
"The supply situation in zinc is precarious. There is a shortage of at least around 40,000 tonnes a year," Shah said. "It will worsen further."
In the week to Wednesday, zinc gained 100 rupees to 7,850 rupees per quintal and copper 50 rupees to 13,550 rupees per quintal.

Nickel, however, lost 300 rupees 36,800 rupees per quintal. Aluminium gained 25 rupees to 7,450 rupees per quintal. Tin and lead were steady at 31,600 rupees per quintal and 4,550 rupees per quintal respectively.
